text: Chapter 1 was honest that a CMDB maintained entirely by hand goes stale fast. Discovery is the real mechanism that solves that at scale: an automated capability built into ServiceNow that scans a network, finds devices and software, and populates or updates CMDB records itself, without a person typing in every field by hand. Everything in this chapter builds from that one idea.

Manual CI entry is accurate the day it's typed in, but nothing keeps it current once something changes and nobody updates the record — a server gets decommissioned, a switch gets racked, and the CMDB never hears about it. Discovery re-runs on a schedule, so it catches new devices, removed devices, and changed specs automatically — the thing manual entry structurally can never do, no matter how disciplined the team typing it in happens to be.

ServiceNow's cloud instance can't see into a customer's network any more than a REST integration can reach an internal system with no public endpoint. Course 7 covered exactly this gap: a MID Server, installed inside the customer's own network, makes outbound-only connections back to the instance, so nothing ever has to open inward through the firewall. Discovery is one of the specific jobs a MID Server exists to carry out — it's the MID Server, not the cloud instance, that actually sends the scan onto the network and relays what it finds back to ServiceNow.

Discovery is genuinely good at infrastructure-level facts: what exists, its specs, what software is installed on it. It is not, by itself, a guarantee of correct ownership, business service relationships, or lifecycle status — that's still the governance work from Chapter 3 and Chapter 5. Discovery keeps the infrastructure layer of the CMDB current with far less manual effort than typing every field by hand; it doesn't remove the need for a human-owned governance process once that data actually exists in the CMDB.

Discovery automates what used to be manual typing, and it needs a MID Server to reach the network at all before it can do any of that. Next: the specific records that control when Discovery runs and which part of the network it scans, and the probes that gather each device's actual details once it's found.
